Selling investments for a cash goal: separate proceeds, cost base and money available to spend

Use a sale-proceeds bridge, cash curve and price stresses to distinguish a holding’s market value from the cash left after selling costs and an assumed tax earmark.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore investment-sale proceeds and a cash goal

Interactive planning lab

Cash earmarked for assumed tax$2,205.56
Cash-goal shortfall after selling$0

One hypothetical CAD holding in a non-registered account, sold proportionately with fractional units allowed. Gain equals proceeds minus proportionate adjusted cost base minus a flat selling cost. The entered percentage applies to the full positive gain as a cash earmark; it is neither a statutory inclusion rate nor a personal marginal rate or tax-return calculation. A loss generates no assumed refund. The sale is capped at the holding value, so an unaffordable target remains a visible shortfall. Tax cash is retained separately and unavailable for the goal. No other income, losses, account rules, settlement delay, FX or price movement during execution.

The central idea

The amount sold, the realized gain and the cash available for a bill are different numbers. Cost base helps calculate the gain; it is not another cash deduction from the sale.

01

Give market value, cost base and the cash goal separate jobs

A statement can show enough market value to cover an upcoming expense without telling you how much must be sold to leave that expense funded. Selling costs and tax-related cash needs can make the required gross sale larger than the bill. A price change before the sale can change the calculation again.

The default uses one hypothetical holding worth CAD 100,000 with a total adjusted cost base of CAD 60,000. The spending goal is CAD 20,000 after a flat CAD 100 selling cost and a separate tax earmark. Fractional units are allowed, so the model can solve a continuous sale amount rather than rounding to a whole number of units.

The CRA describes a capital gain using proceeds, adjusted cost base and selling expenses. This article uses that calculation structure for a capital-property example in a non-registered account. It does not determine whether a real transaction is on capital or income account, and it does not apply to every account wrapper.

02

Allocate cost base to the portion sold

At the selected market value, each dollar of the holding has sixty cents of allocated cost base. Selling 20% of the units would produce CAD 20,000 before costs and allocate CAD 12,000 of cost base to the sold units. The remaining units would retain CAD 48,000 of cost base.

After the CAD 100 selling cost, that particular CAD 20,000 sale has a modeled gain of CAD 7,900: CAD 20,000 minus CAD 12,000 minus CAD 100. The tool then earmarks the entered 25% of that full positive gain, or CAD 1,975. Only CAD 17,925 remains available for the spending goal.

The 25% is an invented effective cash allowance on the full gain. It is neither the statutory inclusion rate nor a personal marginal income-tax rate. Entering a marginal rate directly could misstate the allowance. Actual tax requires the relevant year’s rules, other income and losses, account treatment and the taxpayer’s circumstances.

03

Solve for the sale that leaves the requested cash

Because the first CAD 20,000 sale does not leave CAD 20,000 to spend, the model solves for a larger gross sale. Under the defaults, approximately CAD 22,305.56 must be sold. The allocated cost base is about CAD 13,383.33 and the gain is about CAD 8,822.22.

The separate tax earmark is approximately CAD 2,205.56. The cash reconciliation is CAD 22,305.56 − CAD 100 − CAD 2,205.56 = CAD 20,000, allowing for displayed rounding. The holding retains about CAD 77,694.44 of market value at the unchanged assumed price.

The waterfall does not subtract the CAD 13,383.33 cost base as a cash outflow. That amount represents allocated investment cost used in calculating the gain; it is not another payment made during the sale. Subtracting both cost base and the tax allowance from proceeds would confuse the gain calculation with the cash ledger.

04

Keep the tax cash separate without pretending it has been assessed

The model reserves the assumed tax amount immediately, making it unavailable for the goal. It does not assert that a broker withholds that amount or that the tax is due on the trade date. An earmark is a household planning choice, while an actual payment date belongs on a separate tax cash calendar.

If the selected sale has a loss, the tax earmark is zero. The calculator creates no immediate tax refund and does not apply a loss against another gain. It also excludes loss carryovers, superficial-loss treatment, other account activity, benefits affected by income and any additional consequences of the transaction.

A zero cash goal makes no sale and incurs no fee. A positive sale incurs the flat selling cost, capped at its proceeds. A tiny sale can therefore produce little or no usable cash. Actual trading spreads, percentage commissions or redemption charges would require a different cost function and must not be assumed covered by the single flat input.

05

Hold unit count and cost base fixed when stressing the price

The price-stress bars change the market value by minus 40%, minus 20%, zero and plus 20%, while keeping the same units and total cost base. Each case then solves for the same CAD 20,000 cash goal using the selected fee and tax-earmark percentage.

After a 40% decline, the holding is worth CAD 60,000 and its cost base remains CAD 60,000. The model needs a CAD 20,100 sale, with no positive gain after the selling cost and no tax earmark. That smaller sale amount does not mean the household is wealthier: the price decline has already reduced the whole holding’s market value by CAD 40,000.

For a larger goal, selling the entire holding may still leave a shortage. The main metric reports that shortfall, and the proceeds curve shows when the horizontal goal lies above all achievable cash amounts. The matrix marks a fully funded required sale as unavailable when the holding cannot produce it, instead of displaying a sale larger than the assets owned.

06

Use supported records and a dated funding plan

Replace the market value with a relevant observation and reconcile adjusted cost base from appropriate records. Acquisition costs, reinvestments, returns of capital and other adjustments can make cost base different from the amount originally transferred to an account. The tool accepts an independently established total; it does not reconstruct those records.

All amounts here are CAD and assume one proportionately sold holding. Foreign-currency transactions require their own currency calculations, and a portfolio with several securities requires a decision about which assets are sold. The model does not rank holdings, select tax lots or recommend a security to sell.

Finally, match the expense deadline with the time needed to execute, settle and transfer an actual sale. The calculator assumes cash is available once the sale and earmark are recorded. Its four charts explain the amount reconciliation; a complete plan also needs supported tax assumptions, execution details and a calendar that puts usable cash in place before the bill.
